paras: The plot to lynch William Patterson was a plan by fewer than a dozen citizens of Louisville, Kentucky, to take Patterson, a Black man under sentence of death, from the jail and hang him if Governor Buckner pardoned him. The plan was made public on June 17, 1888, after the governor announced he would not interfere, and Patterson was legally hanged five days later.

Patterson and another Black man, Albert Turner, were convicted of assaulting and fatally beating Jennie Bowman, a servant, in a suburban residence. Turner confessed and was hanged, but on the scaffold he retracted his statement that Patterson had been with him. Patterson denied his guilt, and his conviction was affirmed by the state's highest court.

A petition for a pardon led Buckner to grant a one-month respite and then a second one to June 22, though the Wheeling Intelligencer counted three respites. The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian reported that the governor declined to interfere after a long study of the evidence.

According to the Louisville dispatch, the plotters, described as 'prominent citizens who had taken great interest in the case,' had arranged for one or two men at a time to enter the jail, seize the keys and hang the prisoner. They expected to act so quietly that the authorities could not interfere in time. When the first respite was granted they met to make arrangements, until 'cooler heads' persuaded them the governor would not interfere. No plotter was named.

Patterson was hanged in the Jefferson county jail yard on the morning of June 22, 1888, protesting his innocence. The noose slipped, and he strangled for about four minutes. No report of any action against the plotters appears in the coverage.

The plot is known from a single Louisville dispatch, printed by the Wilmington Daily Republican under the headline 'On the Verge of a Lynching,' which called it 'a strange story' and described the plan without comment on its legality. Wire stories of the hanging, run in the Alexandria Gazette and the Wheeling Intelligencer, did not mention it and instead stressed that 'many people' believed Patterson innocent. The New York Evening World headlined its report 'Died Protesting His Innocence' and called the execution 'a most bunglesome affair.'

Reports differ on the date of the Bowman murder: the Alexandria Gazette gave April 23, 1887, the Wheeling Intelligencer April 23, 1888, and the Evening World 'June 21 a year ago.' The Louisville dispatch placed the crime 'last year,' consistent with 1887.

reader.title: Plot to lynch William Patterson
bases: A2 reports a planned lynching of a condemned Black prisoner by a group of citizens, to be carried out if the governor pardoned him; no attempt was made and Patterson was legally hanged (A5, A6).

The plotters planned to hang Patterson without lawful authority as punishment for the murder of which he had been convicted (A2), but they never acted; Patterson was put to death by legal execution on June 22, 1888 (A5, A6).
The plot rests on one Louisville dispatch printed in the Wilmington Daily Republican (A2); the hanging reports (A4, A5, A6) and the South Kentuckian (A3) do not mention it.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch on the plot
accounts.gist: A small, well-organized group of prominent citizens had fully arranged to take the jail keys and hang Patterson if pardoned, and came close to acting after the first respite.

accounts.label: Wire reports of the execution
accounts.gist: Patterson was legally hanged June 22, protesting innocence, with many believing him innocent; the reports do not mention any plot.

framing.detail: The Daily Republican ran the plot as 'a strange story' under 'On the Verge of a Lynching', reporting the plan matter-of-factly and without condemnation.
Execution stories stressed Patterson's protests of innocence and the bungled hanging ('Patterson Strangled', 'Died Protesting His Innocence').

conflicts.note: A2 says the crime happened 'last year', which rules out 1888; A6's year is likely a typesetting error in the same wire that A4 prints as 1887.

info: Plot made public in Louisville on June 17, 1888; the plotters had met when the first respite was granted, earlier in 1888.
Louisville; the plan targeted the jail where Patterson was held (the Jefferson county jail).
William Patterson, described as 'a negro' / '(colored)', the intended target; not harmed by the plotters.
Convicted, with Albert Turner, of assaulting and fatally beating Jennie Bowman, a servant girl, at a suburban residence; Patterson denied guilt.
'Less than a dozen prominent citizens who had taken great interest in the case'; no names given.
0 by the plotters; Patterson was legally executed on June 22, 1888.
No pardon; Patterson hanged at 6:10 a.m. on June 22, 1888 in the Jefferson county jail yard, protesting his innocence; the drop failed to break his neck and he strangled.

sources.note: 'On the Verge of a Lynching': Louisville dispatch of June 17 reporting that fewer than a dozen prominent citizens had planned to seize the jail keys and hang Patterson if he were pardoned. Only report of the plot found.
quotes: To-day it was learned that a well organized plot had been laid for a few men to lynch Patterson in case he had been pardoned.
Less than a dozen prominent citizens who had taken great interest in the case had fully arranged the plans and in fact they came very near taking this action.
